entries.title: Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing
entries.summary: Technical debt is not necessarily a sign of poor engineering. It can be the price of learning through software in use. As AI accelerates code production beyond our capacity to understand code and context, technical debt increasingly becomes a sociotechnical challenge. By Ben Linders
entries.content:
Technical debt is not necessarily a sign of poor engineering. It can be the price of learning through software in use. As AI accelerates code production beyond our capacity to understand code and context, technical debt increasingly becomes a sociotechnical challenge, Xin Yao noted in her talk "What If Your Biggest Technical Debt Is Social", at GOTO Copenhagen.

Yao quoted Ward Cunningham, who defined debt as "not-quite-right code". Debt sounds like a negative thing, but it can be a deliberate business strategy, she explained:

If we release the code now, well knowing it’s not perfect for the future yet, we’ll get some business feedback, we’ll get some user feedback, we’ll probably get paid for something, and that’s good as a business strategy.

Debt isn’t about poorly written code; it arises when we design software with incomplete knowledge. Hence, debt is the price of learning by doing, Yao argued. Releasing software allows us to test our assumptions against reality. Once we’ve got a learning experience, we have to put that experience back into our code and pay off the debt, she added. The debt becomes problematic when our software doesn’t catch up with our new learning.

Debt can be a good communication strategy toward management. It provides an economic argument for the cost of postponing architectural improvements. However, framing technical debt solely as something to eliminate misses its strategic value. The question is not whether to incur debt, but whether the learning it enables justifies the cost, and whether we actually repay it.

Yao referred to Kent Beck’s article "Earn and Learn," which explores features vs. futures. Features deliver value today, while the future is actually the optionality to adapt those features, Yao explained:

Every bit of code already coded is complexity and a constraint. Every feature removes some future. If you go on producing features, maybe using your LLMs, then at a certain point, all you can do is use your capacity to pay the interest, to fix the code, and you can no longer release features.

The challenge is to balance delivering features with preserving future options, Yao said. Sometimes, delaying a design commitment preserves options until we know more, and this includes postponing some upfront architecture decisions to the last responsible moment as well. As Beck argues, waiting is not laziness; waiting is holding an asset.

Technical debt can therefore be understood as learning made visible in software. We design based on what we know, observe software’s impact, modularity, and its architecture’s implications, and we update our understanding, Yao explained:

The software no longer fits what we now understand, and yesterday’s good understanding becomes today’s debt.

AI introduces a new challenge: software can now be produced faster than teams can develop a shared understanding of its behavior, design decisions and consequences, Yao argued.

Agentic coding makes debt repayment more complex; beyond addressing poorly written AI-generated code, teams must close the gap between what the software actually does and what they understand it to do, while ensuring the code keeps pace with their evolving domain and architectural understanding. Paying off debt is no longer just a technical task, but a sociotechnical one, Yao concluded.

InfoQ interviewed Xin Yao after her talk.

InfoQ: What does learning from technical debt look like, and what benefit does it bring?

Xin Yao: We design and release software based on our best current understanding, then test our assumptions against business and user reality. Paying off debt means incorporating that learning back into the software and closing the gap between what we knew when we released the first iteration and what we know now.

Each iteration creates new debt and new learning. Small batches and tight feedback loops help teams retain the memory of their initial design decisions and continuously repay the old debt with new learning.

InfoQ: What does technical debt look like now that developers are using artificial intelligence?

Yao: With agentic coding, software production can outpace human understanding. Code increasingly becomes a fossil record of agents’ decisions, while humans remain accountable for its consequences. Local productivity gains can create collective costs: more code, weaker ownership and growing gaps in shared understanding.

A study on How Developers Discuss the Burden of AI-Assisted Software Development describes this as "a tragedy of the commons". The danger is not merely more poorly written agentic code, but accelerated learning debt across the sociotechnical system.

entries.title: Presentation: Opening the Black Box: Critical Explainability for AI Agent Tool Selection with Kiji Inspector
entries.summary: Hannes Hapke shares how Dataiku’s open-source Kiji Inspector applies Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) directly to decision tokens to expose why agents pick specific tools. Moving past superficial chain-of-thought narratives, he discusses causal ablation, layer activation extraction via patched vLLM engines, and production monitoring workflows for software architects and senior engineering leaders. By Ha
entries.content:
Transcript

Hannes Hapke: Today we want to open up the black box of our lovely LLMs and agents and want to figure out what to do with them. My name is Hannes. I'm a machine learning engineer. I'm director of engineering at Dataiku, but I also have the great opportunity to run Dataiku's open-source lab, it's called 575 Lab. We work on open-source projects in the responsibility space. I've had the chance to co-author some machine learning publications, and I'm fascinated with machine learning systems, to put them into production, to work on open-source projects. I'm less the research person, I'm more like the person who brings machine learning models into production and building systems around it. I have the great chance to represent 575 Lab here. That is a wonderful organization within Dataiku where we can build open-source tools around responsible AI. Dataiku strongly believes that responsible AI has to be open, so anything that touches privacy or explainability, that is part of our lab.

Anything we share here and anything you will see, it's fully open source. We also contribute to other open-source projects like vLLM, but we have those two signature projects, one is the Kiji Inspector, that's what we're going to demo today, and one is the Kiji Privacy Proxy. If you want to protect your data from leaking to closed source models, that is something you can do, and also you can fine-tune it to your use cases.

The Problem: Opaque Agent Decisions

For today, we want to focus on what we call the Kiji Inspector. It is a tool that is helping you to understand how agents "Think." The fundamental problem that we have with agents is that we don't know how they actually make their decisions. We have a number of tools out there. We have prompt engineering, behavioral testing, or probably the most sophisticated processes like chain of thought. None of them are actually providing you causality, they're often just giving you plausible explanations or plausible narratives of what the root cause could be. When we were asked to figure out how can we make sure that the model that is running an agent is picking the right tool, how do we know that it's thinking about the right context, we decided that we needed to look into the model.

Part I - The Solution

The way we do this is by using sparse autoencoders. Before we get there, let me start explaining what an autoencoder is. This is a concept that has been around for a very long time, probably three decades by now. Autoencoders take a set of inputs, reduce this to a smaller latent space vector, and then reconstruct them through a decoder. The whole point of that autoencoder is that you want to minimize the error between the input and the reconstructed output. In an optimal system, there would be zero error, and the output here would be exactly as the input. Then you know that the representation of your vector z here in your latent space is most optimal. This has been used many times in various things like embeddings and vector searches and information compression, dimensionality reductions of various sorts of kinds. This is a really interesting way of forcing your model to reduce the amount of information to a smaller vector space.

The cool thing about this concept is that it's self-supervised. You don't need any labeling. You use the input as the output, that's your target, and then in between, that's what you would use in production. With sparse autoencoders, you would flip this concept around a little bit. Here in this case, we wouldn't create a bottleneck for the information, but we want to go wide here, with a little catch, and I'll explain the catch. Let's say you grab an activation from a model, or a hidden state, and you pass it through the sparse autoencoder, you can go wide in the information, and that means you force the model to pick certain features to represent the information. When you take a look at the activations inside of a model, there's something that we call polysemantic representation of the context, which means that one neuron that fires can have multiple meanings or topics it would fire on.

In our feature representation, if we want to understand the model, we need to separate them and put them apart from each other, and so that's why we're going wide in the feature representations here. Then again, we try to then have a decoder where we narrow that information piece again, and we try to reconstruct the activations that we used as an input. The catch here is that in this activation function, we are then forcing the model to only use a small set of features to be actually active, and the rest of them, roughly 95%, that's the ideal number, we want to force them to be zero. In that moment, we actually force the model during the training process to just be really selective on a handful of features, and then we can be absolutely certain that those features are representing the themes and the context of the model itself, what the model was thinking in this given layer at the processing of a certain token.

Then we can go one step further. Once you have those feature vectors you generated, those indices don't mean anything to us, to humans. What we can then do is, once we have a corpus, we can grab all the documents that fire highly on, let's say, dimension 3 and dimension 6, and then we can look at those documents and say, what do they have in common? It could easily be that they say like, the first one has something to do with Python, so then over the course of the entire corpus, we could say, those two features, they represent a programming language or an API vocabulary or things like this.

What we have tried to do in this project is combining a number of things and package them up so that everybody can use them in production. The first thing that we want to do is, sparse autoencoders have been around for a number of years now, and OpenAI published some research, and Eleuther published some research on this, but they focused on the entire LLM generation. What we changed here in our approach is we were only interested in the agentic decision-making. We focused on the decision token rather than the entire prompt, and then averaging those activations across the entire prompt. Then we put a bunch of concepts together. For example, Eleuther came out with this concept of token-level fuzzing, and so we added this to our framework so anybody who wants to use that framework and trains their own models, they can use that token testing. Then also we added causal validation testing as well so that you can make sure, is it actually causal or is it just correlation?

Then the other sweet thing, what we changed here in this project, what is novel, is that we're not just training on a number of prompts, but we created those pairs, training pairs. We have a given intent — I'll show you an example later — but for a given intent, you have something that we call the anchor that's the correct answer and the correct tool use, and then there's an adversarial reply, which is very similar, but very different. It's basically like look something up in an internal database versus look up something online. Two different use cases, very similar in the prompt response, but very different outcome in terms of the tool selection.

Looking at the training pipeline, let's say we have all these pairs generated, which I will show you how we do this. We then take our target model, and little caveat here, those have to be open-source models. We can't do this with OpenAI's models because we don't have access to their weights, but you can do this with any open-source model, and that's another novelty in our framework that we're not just focusing on Gemma models from Google or Nemotron models from NVIDIA. That tool, that framework here is working with various open-source models that are out there. You pick your subject model, that's the model you want to use the explainability for, and then you run all your prompts through the model itself, grab all the activations from the particular layers you want to watch. Then with those activations, you can train your sparse autoencoder as I just showed you with putting them in, widening them up, and then forcing the decoder again to reconstruct that activation.

Then once you have the model trained, you can do a contrastive analysis, and I'll show you this later, how we then figure out through those pairs of what's actually relevant in the context or not. Or you can go to a large language model and say, tell me what those documents have in common, and then you can generate those themes. This all happens in that package where we call the Kiji Inspector. You put in your corpus, you nominate those models, and out you get a feature definition of what those features mean when you run those LLMs and agent requests.

Earlier, I just mentioned you have to pick a certain layer. There's a little bit of an art what layer to pick rather than science. There's a little bit of an explanation here that if you're early in the stack, like maybe in the first third, the model hasn't fully conceptualized all the concepts of your prompt request. You're basically activating things that are highly relevant to the prompt itself. If you're further down the stack, there's a lot of intricacies of the model itself. Here in this particular model, we're looking at the Nemotron 3 from NVIDIA. That's an MoE model. That's because every different request goes through different routings, you have crazy errors. Learning something later on is very difficult. Also, the concepts you extract are so abstract in some cases that even for humans, it's impossible to understand what's going on. Then also for the models, it's difficult.

What we wanted to do is, for our particular experiments, we picked layer 20 because it is already down the pipe. It's like the model extracted some abstract concepts. It's not too far down the pipe that it would be too non-human understandable. In our open-source models, what we're publishing, we're publishing multiple layers. You can pick wherever you want to be in your model layer setup. Again, this is another representation of the training pipeline. Basically, you have your input. You calculate those representations. Then you do the reconstruction back to, in our case, it's 2688 dimensions. Then you calculate the loss. It's a very standard autoencoder model architecture. The key thing, and we show this in the following slide, we're using a particular activation, what we call the Jump Regularized Linear Unit. I will explain this here why this is in this particular case.

Then, how do we actually focus on the decision token? The way we do this is by forcing the agent to respond to a given prompt and says, I will use blank. Whatever tool, whatever the model then responds is expected to be the tool name, because we've provided the selection of tools in the prompt itself. Then in the response, we would see what tool the model has chosen. We do this a million times. We generated a training set with a million samples, basically 500,000 pairs, good and bad examples. The pairs come in later when we try to evaluate the model. During the training process itself, we use them raw, and we have those 1 million samples. Why are we doing this contrastive pair design again? Here's a little example. Let's say you have a given intent, resolve a password issue, and you can have the request, how do I reset my password?

That would trigger the tool knowledge base. You could also say, I tried to reset my password three times, and that could be a completely different tool. It's very similar in the response or in the request, but it's a very different tool outcome in this particular case. Later on, what you will see is we will then use those pairs and figure out which of the features we generated are actually relevant for those given tools. When we generate the features for both tools, the dimensions where the features are different have mostly contributed to the decision-making between knowledge base versus ticket lookup.

I don't want to go through the math here, but there's an interesting concept regarding the JumpReLU. As you know, Regularized Linear Units basically are, anything negative is zeroed out and anything positive is the input. It's like a linear function, but it's not differentiable because of that bend. Here in the JumpReLU, that's another derivative of the ReLU activation function. It's basically the output is the input, but there's a threshold. The interesting thing here is when we train the model of, figure out which activation is actually relevant and not relevant, we can then tune that threshold during the training process as the output activation. That's another tweak we can have to teach the model which feature is relevant for which given activation. When we look at some results per layer, then we see some really interesting side effects of early on, the error is low, but the model hasn't learned much.

Later on, the error is crazy high because this is logarithmic. Then we have too many, basically we learn something, but the error is exorbitant high. That's why we ended up in our practical example, we ended up somewhere in between at layer 20. Again, if we look at some stats here, like total, I think we had like 2,600-and-something input features, we widened this to 10,000 dimensions. Of those 10,000 dimensions, a little bit above 80% of those dimensions are alive. That means somewhere through the training, they have been nonzero. Then only less than 0.2% are completely dead, meaning those features have never been used through the entire training process. Then when we do the testing later on, we actually figured out that out of those 10,000 features, 668 are actually highly relevant to all the tool selections we wanted to investigate. This is for a given model for a given layer and a given dataset. If you retrain this, you might see different results.

Then somebody could say, why do we have to go through all this craziness of sparse autoencoders and training another machine learning model in all these crazy setups? As you can imagine, it's a lot of computation there. This is basically a couple comparisons. If you take the activations and then train a linear model on this, could we then figure out is this tool correct or incorrect? If you compare this and a binary classification here, we get to almost 80% accuracy. It's not bad, but it's also not perfect. Then if you do some just accuracy versus F1 score, that's a little bit lower. Then somebody could say, what happens if we just take those activations with those 2,000 dimensions and we just cluster them? Could we from the cluster then figure out which tool is the correct one? You're better off flipping a coin than actually clustering.

I think that was for us the interesting thing to see with the sparse autoencoders. I'll explain what fuzzing is. We can bridge the gap between interpretability and also having some causality testable features. I just mentioned token-level fuzzing. That was introduced by Eleuther sometime back when they looked into sparse autoencoders for entire prompts. What they did was they took a look at the prompt and then swapped out individual tokens, and then looked at how is the activation affected by swapping out those tokens and how is the end result being affected by that. That's the same concept we provide in our tool case here, in our framework that people can use when they want to evaluate their sparse autoencoders. Then when you look at the individual features and the quality of them, we can see that for the majority of the features they actually correlate really well to what we predicted the outcome to be. Only a small number of them have very poor influence on the overall decision-making. Again, from those 600 features we selected, it felt pretty good. This is heading in the right direction.

Part II - The Causality Test

Then, let's take a look at causality and those other things. That's always the big question. We started this project where like, can we explain how an agent selected a tool? At some point, we needed to take a look at, can we actually prove causality? Little side note, I'm not a statistician, so I would love to have a better conversation about this with somebody who is more experienced with this. What we have done is looking at the activations. While the activation in this given layer in the model was produced, we then zeroed out the top 10 activations in that given vector. Then we looked at, is the tool selection changing or not? This was our setup. It's a little bit of like wiring and intercepting all the activations and those types of things. Don't worry, through the framework, we provide the other tools where you can replicate that.

The way this works is for our experiment setups here, where we looked at various tools, we were actually able to show that if you do the contrastive ablation, that worked extremely well for a number of tools. There were certain tools where we couldn't prove it, but for the majority of the tools, it actually looked very promising. Just a couple results here, the p-score is very low, so we were pretty happy about this. Through those testing, we were able to show that 23 of those contrast types actually worked. That worked better than randomly flipping. We felt that this is also, again, heading in the right direction. Like, yes, those particular activations, those 10 dimensions we blanked out or zeroed out actually contributed actively to the tool selection.

Part III - Using Kiji Inspector

This was a lot of theory and a little bit of math and all those types of things, but you don't have to do this yourself, and that's why we have the Kiji Inspector, and that's why we open sourced that at Dataiku. What we're trying to provide here with a toolkit and the framework is like, we wanted to provide a model-agnostic framework that everybody else can use in the industry. Companies like Google have published similar frameworks, but they're always very tool specific. For example, Gemma Scope is the explainability tool for Gemma 2 or Gemma 3 or Gemma 4, or there's no Gemma 4 expanded model yet. There is no training pipeline. There's a lot of repos floating around with scripts and everything, but it's not like something you can download and fork and run something end-to-end on your site for your particular models and your particular use cases.

Then we wanted to provide a full production setup. We see a lot of research in those cases, but we hadn't seen a good production setup where people can run vLLMs and also get the activations back. Because in most setups like vLLM or SGLang, you get the response back but those inference tools don't give you the activations of a particular layer back. We provide a patch to vLLM that allows you to do that, and we also give you the containers so you can run this in production. Then as I said, everything is fully open source. We provide Docker containers, there's a PyPI package as you will see, and then all the models we have trained are on Hugging Face. This is only a subset, the list is way longer of what we're providing on Hugging Face. With our large training set of those 1 million data points or 1 million samples and the 500,000 pairs, we recently just trained Gemma 4.

Who knows if Google actually comes out with their sparse autoencoders. We wanted to beat them, and so we have the sparse autoencoders for the Gemma 4 and then for the latest Nemotron models, the Nemotron 3, we also provide the sparse autoencoders. Unfortunately, we don't have infinite compute resources as Google, that's why we have to pick certain layers to support them. If you have specific reasons, and you want a particular layer of a particular model, let us know, we can probably help you there as well.

How would the inference setup look like? If you run for example an agent and says, analyze my Q3 report, you would go through a large language model. Again, it has to be an open-source model, because you have to host that model so you can patch your vLLM version. We're hoping to get this into vLLM at some point so that hosting platforms like Baseten and others can provide those features as well. Then, you not just get the response back but you also get the activation vector for a given layer for your response. Then that goes into your sparse autoencoder. From your 2688 dimensions, you would then go up to 10,000 dimensions. Remember most of the dimensions are actually zero. Then you can take a look at the top features that are active in this large vector, and then you can take a look at those indices and figure out what are the themes you have determined during the training itself.

Then you can take those themes and put them back into a large language model as an explanation. Now somebody might ask, what's the difference now between doing all of this and chain of thought? The key difference is this information piece was directly derived from the activation during the model when that token was generated. It is not chain of thought where it first goes through some reasoning steps and then tries to execute. In chain of thought it could say like, here are two things I want to do, and then it executes 15 other things. There's no connection between those two steps. Here, there's the direct connection between the activation at a given layer. It goes into the sparse vector, and then we have the connection to the feature map we generated during the training.

How does it work in production if you want to use this? We've generated this PyPI package called the Kiji Inspector. Until recently you also had to update your transformer libraries for Gemma 4, but all the Gemma 4 changes lined it so you can use the latest library here. Then the setup is very straightforward. If you're familiar with Hugging Face, that's how you would infer a model. In our case we define like a Gemma model. We give our given prompt. This is like a home repair thing. "My dishwasher is smelly. What should I do?" Then we define our layer. The Gemma 4 model, this is the E4B model that's a little bit smaller so we go a little bit earlier in the stack. In this case we use layer 8. That setup is standard cookie cutter. The only difference, what I would point out is like, if your GPU supports bfloat16, use it. It's just an inference. You don't train anything so just save the memory for your inference. Then again this is just standard prompt stuff. Nothing special here. Nothing unique. Very boilerplate Hugging Face code.

Now the actually fun part starts. In Hugging Face, you can define what we call forward hooks. When the model is being executed, in Hugging Face the model is not compiled so you can easily hook into the execution, and say, give me the vector of a given layer for that given input. Then, we can grab the layer from here. When it's being executed, we can then actually ship it back to the response and send it to the user. I can show you another setup we have where you can also work with compiled models so you get a better performance. Then you run the inference, you retrieve the vector, and that is your activation. You're ready to go to use your sparse autoencoder. If you use one of the models we already support, you can then use our Kiji Inspector. We followed the Hugging Face setup. You can say like, from pre-trained, you mention the base model and under the hood we figure out like, what sparse autoencoder it needs to download.

We go to the correct repo, and then we use the correct model for the correct layer. Under the hood we convert this into the correct feature vector and then also do the lookup of the features to the themes. When you run SAE describe, that's how you get the description and not just a random vector. This is how it looks like, and I will show you this, again, but this is a little bit better readable. You see all the indices up here, they basically tell you what indices is the top five the ones that are firing. You see the number one it says unknown. What does it mean? It means like during the training, that feature in that feature vector was not of high importance and we haven't described that. Maybe we need more training data or maybe we need to tweak the training process. The interesting thing is that when we look at the second feature that was firing, it was actually something related to dishwasher gasket issues.

Seems relevant to the prompt we have. If it would fire on something completely unrelated here then there would be a good sign to go back and say like, maybe there's something going on in the model or maybe my prompt is incorrect or something else happening. Those are the things you can then see from the inspection and the data we provide through the package.

Demo - Kiji Inspector, Live

Let me show you here a little demo of how this would work and how you can actually use this in production. Again, this is the same code that I showed you earlier where we just stepped through. I pre-ran this in a Colab notebook. If you want to follow along you can go to our GitHub repo. The quick start example works in a free Colab. If you want to use a larger model you have to pay for the bigger GPUs nowadays. This is still giving you an overview of how this works under the hood. Here's a truncated information on the slide. You see some more information, and we also provide the bottom examples. Basically, here you see all the things that are least related to that request. Then you can go down, and you can turn this into a description and you can see what the confidence level is.

Here's another thing that I think could be really interesting for folks. As I mentioned at the beginning, we provide patches for vLLM. Here in this case is like you can also execute the whole thing in vLLM. When you do vLLM generate, you can then also get the same vectors back with the explanations. We tied this all together in vLLM. Then we have another interesting example I think that is a use case where we're stepping through a larger agent setup. Instead of going through the code I want to show you how the result could look like, and maybe that gives you a feeling of how you can use this in your product. We built the standalone demo of like, this is your home repair agent. It tells you if something is broken, can you fix it yourself? Should you call somebody else? It could potentially look up YouTube videos of how to fix it.

In order to make sure that we know what the agent is doing, for every agent step, we then also look up what the sparse autoencoder features are. Here in this particular case, this was the dishwasher example, it relates to a machine handling water I would think, washing machines, and there's something like old machine troubling. At least we know that the agent is heading in the right direction when it made the decision of like a dishwasher is leaking in this particular case. You can do this for every different tool call. This one is completely empty, it's a good example, because when we trained this there was not a tool call in the training set at all for YouTube videos. For us it will be a good sample of like, we need to add more real-world examples in our training set. I showed you this example. There's a couple more, there's a left example there as well where we show this in a live demo, you can follow along what the agent is doing in the frontend while the agent is figuring out what is actually happening. It's pretty fun to look at.

What are the particular use cases you can use for your applications and where you could use the Kiji Inspector. One thing is like you could figure out what an agent misbehavior would be. Anything that is like, has it picked the wrong tool, as I showed you earlier in the examples, that is a something. You can do it for audit compliance. Some companies looking at this and figuring out, it's like, if we have another track record, traces is one thing but explainability is another thing. When we do traces, we basically see what tool has been selected but we still can't explain why that tool was selected. Here we generate another set of logs and figuring out why the agent has particularly selected this tool that is shown in the traces. Then we can do validate of prompt engineering. If you're not quite sure, like you want to optimize your prompt for particular goals and you don't want to do this iterative loop, you can then also investigate like how is that tool responding to your given prompt based on the activations.

Then obviously monitoring production drift. If your data changes, let's say you test your agent with a set of prompts, you watch those activations, and then over time you can see if those activations change. That is a really good indication that the data that is going through that agent has changed. Maybe you should take a look at that as well.

Key Takeaways

Just to summarize this, what are the key takeaways? We have the chance to prove that sparse autoencoders can work to explain why the agent made a certain decision. We showed how the token-level fuzzing works, and as part of the package we can prove that tweaking those prompts lead to different activations. I also showed the causal evidence of the tool selection is affected by zeroing out certain activations in the model itself. Then we did some comparison with construction only baseline, meaning, because it's a decoder and there's a loss effect, if we take this out, then we can actually show that there's a causal effect in the sparse autoencoder.

Limitations and Future Directions

I want to let you go with a couple limitations and also pointing out some future work. As I said, you do need the model itself. It doesn't work with closed source models. Hopefully at some point they give us similar tools on there, and that would be fantastic. The training is pretty compute intensive, especially if you want to create your own datasets. If you want to use the tool and you want to create your own training sets, come talk to us. We can share some more tricks and tips of how to run this effectively. As I mentioned earlier, it is a synthetic dataset. If anybody wants to use this and has some ideas of what is missing in the dataset and where should we go in terms of making it more real-world replicable, then let us know. We would love to collaborate on that as well.

There's a future work here. We want to support more open-source models and provide those models from the start through Hugging Face. Something that is on mind is currently Qwen. More multi-layer experiments. Currently everything is based on single layers. It could be really interesting if you take a layer from the first third and then a layer from the last third, and then combine those and see what actually happens. Then another interesting idea we had was like what happens if you do cross-model transfer. Basically, you train on a Gemma model. You take those vectors. You learn certain features. Is there something we can generalize then if we go to another model and so we see certain patterns. That is all future work. We haven't touched this yet. If anybody wants to collaborate on this let me know. Everything is fully open source. We live from contribution from others. This is not our project. It's a community project.

Questions and Answers

Participant 1: Is there anything that stops this from being applied to something by the training, of course, beyond tool calls. For example, if we were looking at safety alignment. The reason being that at least from the results of the causal inspection that you did, it seems to be possible to do some kind of steering after you train the model. Do you have any insight on any ways that we could possibly change something like this for alignment and then use that for active steering after deployment.

Hannes Hapke: I think there's nothing that I would say that it's not possible. One of the things we're looking into is the security aspects of like, can we detect malicious attacks in those activations? Yes, I think that's possible. I think from the research I showed earlier when I showed the clustering versus linear classification versus the sparse autoencoder, it was visible to me. I think to me that's sort of the proof that if you just look at their pure activations you can't figure out what is going on. You do need the step through the sparse autoencoder. Yes, nothing is limited to just a tool call. For us, it was like a feasible project scope. The team is pretty small, so for us it felt feasible. Yes, totally.

Participant 2: Do you have any real-world examples where using your approach gave you a different understanding of why a tool was selected versus using chain of thought tells?

Hannes Hapke: Yes, we have a bunch of anecdotal examples. We haven't summarized them yet into something scientific that we say here's my prompt and here's my analysis. Chain of thought was maybe a bit abstract. Then in the features, we could see like, this is actually looking for a particular problem. For example, this dishwasher repair thing, it picked water damage on an electrical equipment or something. It felt more precise than the actual chain of thought. There's a little caveat. The sparse autoencoder we trained for those examples, they were domain specific. Meaning that we were focusing on a very particular specific domain and that's what we built the training set for. There was a little bit of an unfair advantage. Also, it changes with model size. If you use a smaller model like the Gemma E4B, I think those interpretability tools have a benefit of it. Those were the two things where you could see the difference between the chain of thought versus the explainability tool.

Participant 2: For those who are stuck with the closed source proprietary models, could you imagine surrogate models working ok enough? Do you think that the closed and open-source models are similar enough with why they would make certain choices?

Hannes Hapke: I can't speak for OpenAI and others. I would think the models are bigger than what we see in the open-source world obviously. I think you have maybe a better chain of thought experiments. That's an interesting question. We should compare different prompts and run them through a large Qwen model versus a large like OpenAI 5.5, and then look at the thinking steps, and see, are they comparable or not? Generally, we will never see this technology in closed source models, because, A, I think all the companies are walking back their logics now, because through the logics you could figure out model internals. This is even more like internals. They never want to share this. The other thing is also like, yes, it's proprietary modeling. They don't want to really open source that or share that.

entries.title: Azure Logic Apps Standard Gets a Local CLI in Preview
entries.summary: Microsoft has released a public preview of the logicapp extension for the Azure CLI, adding local project creation, workflow authoring, a runtime lifecycle, connector management, run inspection, and test scaffolding for Logic Apps Standard, work that previously required the VS Code extension. The product team pitches the terminal surface as determinism for AI-assisted development. By Steef-Jan Wig
entries.content:
Microsoft has released a public preview of a local command-line interface for Azure Logic Apps Standard, shipped as the logicapp extension for the Azure CLI. It adds project creation, workflow authoring, a local runtime, connector and connection management, run inspection, and test scaffolding to a tool that until now only managed deployed apps, so that a Standard workflow can be created, run, and tested without Visual Studio Code.

The extension installs automatically the first time an az logicapp developer command runs on Azure CLI 2.67.0 or later, and adds 19 command groups with 64 commands beside the thirteen existing cloud-management commands, which it leaves untouched. On the authoring side, project create creates or adopts a local project; workflow create, set, export, and validate work on individual workflow.json files with offline validation by default, and runtime start, stop, and show manage a local host on port 7071, launching the Azurite storage emulator when the project is configured for development storage.

The remaining groups reach into running and deployed apps. connector and connection inspect built-in and managed connectors and wire connections into a project or a deployed app, run and trigger history start, wait on, cancel and resubmit executions and download an action’s recorded inputs and outputs, and deployment package produces what the documentation calls a deterministic deployment package. Named context shortcuts hold a target so later commands do not repeat it.

(Source: Microsoft Community Hub)

The doctor and test commands say the most about who the tool expects to be typing. runtime doctor only reads: project files, tool versions, cached bundle evidence, loopback ports. It "never installs, downloads, starts, stops, repairs, decrypts settings, changes context, or contacts cloud storage," and it exits 1 for a required failure and 2 when a required check comes back unknown. Testing is split into three steps for the same reason. test create scaffolds a native SDK test project and stops before restoring a package or running anything, test plan writes a preflight report without executing a test, and test run is the only command that builds and runs them, under a deadline. The announcement lists limitations on that last step. In the pull request that added the extension, author Riley Evans goes further: native SDK test code is trusted rather than sandboxed, and the agent bootstrap command does not exist yet.

Sagar Sharma, a Microsoft MVP, wrote on LinkedIn that this is deliberate. The CLI is "literally pitched as adding determinism to local AI-assisted coding": an agent validates, runs, inspects and tests, then repeats until the run is green, and secrets reach it through stdin rather than on the command line. Sharma had already called the CLI the sleeper hit of Microsoft's recent Logic Apps announcements in an earlier write-up, on the grounds that an agent without a deterministic way to validate and run a workflow is guessing. Named contexts, capability discovery and the handling of secrets were his evidence that someone had designed for that case.

Sonny Gillissen, also a Microsoft MVP, put the same point in terms of a team's week. A new hire clones a repository and has a local runtime up "in minutes, instead of hours." A coding assistant drafting a workflow from a business requirement works "with an authoritative shell instead of assumptions." Integration flows get tested from the CI/CD pipeline instead of by hand. He called the CLI a bridge from today's development process to a fully automated one and, in passing, said an agent could test a workflow locally "without ever touching Azure at all."

That passing remark is the one Christos Panagiotidis, a Microsoft MVP and certified trainer, would test first. His pilot plan is explicitly a proposal rather than a report of a run, and its two main cautions come straight from Microsoft's own walkthrough. That walkthrough uses live Azure and Microsoft 365 resources, and some of its commands change deployed connections, so a local run has remote effects, whatever the terminal suggests.

Microsoft itself notes that validation "does not establish authorization or business correctness." Panagiotidis adds a housekeeping point: CLI extensions do not update with the CLI, so anyone comparing results across runs needs the CLI, extension, runtime and project versions recorded next to each result.

Microsoft has said a broader command surface will follow soon. Until then, the designer stays in VS Code. The CLI edits workflow.json directly; it cannot change the state of a running local app, and the pull request's own limits section concedes that Linux CI results prove neither native SDK execution nor execution against live Azure.

entries.title: Google Open-Sources TPU Sync for KV Cache and Weight Transfer on TPUs
entries.summary: Google Cloud has open-sourced TPU Sync, a native C++ library that moves KV cache blocks and model weights between TPU HBM, host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network. By Daniel Dominguez
entries.content:
Google Cloud has open-sourced TPU Sync, a native C++ library that moves KV cache blocks and model weights between TPU HBM, host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network. GCP also announced the TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max systems, the project targets two workloads where accelerators often wait on data: long-context and disaggregated LLM serving, and reinforcement learning loops that push updated weights from trainers to rollout samplers.

For prefill/decode disaggregation, Google says median KV transfer latency for Qwen3 235B fell from several seconds to about 230 ms, with average TTFT reductions of 60% for that model and 90% for a 480B model at low concurrency. For prefix caching, it reports up to 90% lower average TTFT on 64K-context workloads.

Developers get Python wheels for JAX and PyTorch, with KV cache manager, KV store, and weight synchronizer APIs. TPU Sync acts as the KV connector for vLLM-TorchTPU through vLLM's KVConnector interface, as the disaggregation and hierarchical-cache backend for SGLang-TorchTPU, and pairs with llm-d 1.0 on GKE for prefix-cache-aware routing. The RL weight-sync module for Pathways and multi-controller JAX is experimental. The GitHub repository, which absorbed the earlier TPU Raiden codebase, warns that APIs are changing rapidly and that only development builds are on PyPI, and recommends pinning to its last-known-good commit. It is validated on TPU v7x and v6e, and the PyTorch wheel requires a matching torch_tpu build that is not on a public index.

On GPUs, similar problems are handled by NVIDIA Dynamo and its NIXL transfer library, LMCache, which offloads KV cache to CPU memory, disk, or remote stores, Mooncake, the KVCache-centric serving architecture behind Moonshot AI's Kimi, and vLLM's own disaggregated prefill connectors. TPU Sync differs mainly in being tied to PJRT and TPU tile layouts, and in covering RL weight transfer in the same library.

Early reactions focused on data movement rather than the new chips, with developer Anand Butani sharing:

TPU sync cutting kv transfer latency 90% matters more to me than the chip names, long-context serving mostly dies on moving cache between nodes.

Another developer posting under the pseudonym @lgoodbookd ran rough numbers on why bandwidth alone does not solve the problem:

8i Max doubles HBM bandwidth to ~17.2TB/s, yet one 64K session on a 235B MoE still eats ~12.6GB of KV cache. That's why open-sourcing TPU Sync (host-DRAM KV tiering, ~223GB/s per v7x host) may matter as much as the new package. Bandwidth helps; capacity is still the wall.

TPU Sync is available under the Apache 2.0 license, and its repository includes architecture documentation, C++ and Python APIs, and examples for single-host and multi-host disaggregated serving and host KV offloading. Until a stable release is cut, the JAX and PyTorch packages are published only as development builds, while the storage tier and RL weight synchronization remain experimental

entries.title: Author Q+A: finprim is a Case for One Financial Validation Library in TypeScript
entries.summary: finprim is an MIT-licensed TypeScript library that offers IBAN, BIC, card, sort code, VAT, routing number and loan functions through one API with no runtime dependencies. Its author built it after duplicated validators drifted apart across web and mobile. It validates and formats data only, and does not process payments. He is cautious about adding SEPA and ACH file generation. By Daniel Curtis
entries.content:
finprim, which is an MIT-licensed TypeScript library that puts IBAN, BIC, card, sort code, VAT, routing number and loan calculations behind one API, has published its fifth release, 0.1.4. The repository has 81 stars.

InfoQ asked author Oluwatosin Adelaja what pushed him to build it, and where he wants it to stop.

InfoQ: What pushed you to build finprim?

Adelaja: Honestly, it came from doing the same work too many times. At Sprint Technology Solutions we had several products, and each one ended up with its own copy of the same financial validation, sort code checks in one place, IBAN formatting in another, card validation somewhere else, all written slightly differently by whoever got there first.

The moment it really landed for me was on a payout flow. We had account and sort code validation on the web side, and then the mobile app needed the same thing. Rather than share it, the validation got rewritten for mobile, and the two copies drifted. One of them was a little stricter than the other, so a bank detail that the web form accepted would get rejected on mobile, and we had people re-entering details that were actually fine. It took longer than it should have to track down, because nobody thinks to check whether two "identical" validators are actually identical. The fix was easy once we found it, but the real problem was that there were two of them at all.

I hit the same shape of thing again later building a daily pay feature for NHS workers, where the same rules needed to hold on web and on mobile. That is when I stopped treating it as a one-off chore and started thinking it should just be one library, written once and tested once, that any product could pull in and trust.

InfoQ: What was missing that justified a unified library rather than assembling existing single-purpose packages?

Adelaja: You can absolutely wire together a pile of single-purpose packages, and plenty of teams do. The problem is what you are left maintaining. Each package has its own API shape, its own types, its own idea of what a valid result looks like, and often its own dependencies. So you end up writing a layer of glue code just to make them agree with each other, and that glue becomes its own thing to test and keep working.

finprim's bet is that financial validation is coherent enough to live behind one consistent API. The same shape of input, the same shape of result, and the same typing approach across IBAN, sort code, card, VAT, all of it. And zero runtime dependencies, so there is no tree of other people's packages to audit or keep patched. For something sitting in the path of a payment, I wanted fewer moving parts, not more.

InfoQ: What concrete class of bugs do branded types prevent, and why not rely on plain runtime validation?

Adelaja: The bug class is the one where a string that was never validated gets used as if it had been. To the compiler, a validated IBAN and a random string are both just a string, so nothing stops you passing the wrong one into a function that assumes the value is good. It compiles fine, and then it fails at runtime, which in this domain means it fails in the middle of a live transaction.

Branded types close that gap. A validated IBAN comes back as its own distinct type, not a plain string, so if you try to use an unchecked value where a validated one is required, the compiler rejects it before the code ever runs. The runtime validation still happens, that does not go away. The branding just guarantees it actually happened and that nobody quietly skipped it on some code path. It moves a whole class of "we forgot to validate this one route" mistakes from production back to compile time.

InfoQ: For something handling payment data, how do you think about trust, what can you guarantee, and where do you draw the line?

Adelaja: The honest answer starts with being clear about what finprim is and is not. It validates and formats financial data. It does not store anything, it does not send anything over the network, and it does not process payments. No database, no telemetry, no outbound calls.

So the guarantees I can actually make are narrow and specific. It checks values against published standards, IBAN structure, checksum rules, card network ranges, and tells you whether they are well formed, deterministically, without logging the sensitive values it is handling. That last part is deliberate. You do not want account numbers or card numbers turning up in logs, so the library does not put them there.

Where I draw the line matters just as much. finprim does not tell you a payment is safe to make, it is not a compliance tool, and it is not a replacement for the checks your payment provider runs. It confirms the data is shaped correctly before it goes anywhere. Treating a validation library as more than that would be the real mistake.

InfoQ: How do you source and maintain the correctness of 80+ IBAN formats, VAT quirks and card ranges, and how is it tested?

Adelaja: The rules come from the published standards rather than from me guessing. IBAN is checked against the ISO 13616 country formats, card numbers use Luhn plus the published network ranges, VAT uses the documented per-country formats, and so on. Where there is an authoritative spec, that is the source of truth.

On testing, each validator runs against known-good and known-bad values taken from those reference sources, so the tests check behaviour against the standard, not just against themselves. Overall coverage is around 91% of lines and 88% of statements. The core validation modules are the most heavily covered, the IBAN, card, VAT, routing, BIC and sort code logic sits around 94% of lines with full function coverage, and the thinner coverage is in the optional React bindings rather than the validation itself. I would rather be straight about that split than quote one headline number, because the part that actually handles financial data is the part that is tested hardest.

Keeping it correct over time is mostly manual, I update the formats as the standards change, and this is one place the outside contributors have genuinely helped, because people using it in different countries spot edge cases I would never hit on my own.

InfoQ: SEPA and ACH generation is a big jump from validation into transaction generation. Where do you want finprim to end up?

Adelaja: That is a fair thing to push on, because generation is a genuinely different job from validation, and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Validating an IBAN is self-contained. Producing a SEPA credit transfer file or an ACH batch means taking on formatting rules, sequencing and a lot more responsibility for getting something exactly right that is going to be submitted to a bank.

Where I want finprim to sit is as a validation and formatting toolkit first. I am deliberately cautious about the generation side. If it does move into producing standard file formats, I would want that to be safe, well-tested generation of documented formats, not finprim turning into a transaction engine or a payments platform. I would rather it did one layer really well than spread itself thin doing a half version of what a payment provider already gives you.

Narrower tools exist, such as ibankit for IBAN and BIC alone, and on DEV a commenter called the Dinero.js approach solid while warning that teams get burned when a library's precision assumptions diverge from the processor's.

Adelaja is a senior full stack engineer. All five releases have stayed within 0.1.x, so upgrading has meant patch releases rather than code changes, and there is no dedicated migration guide, so the README and release notes are the reference.

entries.title: LinkedIn Replaces Argo CD with a Custom GitOps Engine for Kubernetes Deployments
entries.summary: In a recent post, LinkedIn revealed it has replaced Argo CD with its own GitOps engine. This new system deploys applications across over 250 Kubernetes clusters. It supports more than 4,000 services and manages over 100,000 deployments each week. By Claudio Masolo
entries.content:
In a recent post, LinkedIn revealed it has replaced Argo CD with its own GitOps engine. This new system deploys applications across over 250 Kubernetes clusters. It supports more than 4,000 services and manages over 100,000 deployments each week. According to a post, deployment infrastructure failures fell from 925 to 63 despite a 3.7x increase in deployment volume. The median time to detect and conclude a failed deployment dropped from 16.1 to 2.45 minutes.

LinkedIn started with one Argo CD instance per cluster, a topology it chose because Argo CD already managed its cluster add-ons that way. Clusters run up to 5,000 nodes each. A central deployment orchestrator spawned an ephemeral pod per deployment, with Argo CD hidden behind it. The team lists seven problems that emerged at scale. Argo CD doesn't have an 

observedGeneration
, so you can't link sync and health status to a specific deployment. LinkedIn created a Lua health check that uses a tracking annotation to address this. A Synced and Healthy application could also resolve to an unintended revision when stale repo-server cache entries were used.

Two of the issues were architectural. Argo CD maintains one watch per group-version-resource across Applications. LinkedIn’s clusters have low resource-type diversity. This means etcd churn from one app can slow syncs for all apps. In one test, sync took under 3 minutes on a cluster with 60,000 pods and over 10 minutes with more than 80,000. The second was server-side-apply PATCH. Kubernetes truncates managedFields once an object has had more than 10 distinct field managers, and the API server then forgets who owns a field. In LinkedIn's AI workloads, which run multiple containers per Pod, a container removed from a manifest could therefore survive on the live Pod. The team had pruning disabled because destructive operations in production require approval. The remaining problems were CRD schema changes that required controller restarts across the fleet. Some OutOfSync states did not reflect real drift. Error messages were buried in boilerplate.

LinkedIn evaluated Flux but found it shared the same controller paradigm, so it built the engine as a library. Each deployment runs in its pod, with no shared controller state. Updates use PUT for full replacements, not PATCH. They retry on 

resourceVersion
conflicts with exponential backoff. A 3-way diff across the live object, the previously deployed manifest, and the newly rendered manifest detects drift, and genuine drift fails the deployment. The same pod then watches the object's status until it converges or times out, and the API server unwraps errors for the user. Objects missing from the rendered manifest become deletion candidates, subject to delete protection, and convergence logic for LinkedIn's CRDs is built in.

The comparison uses the same calendar month a year apart. The migration ran from July 2025 to April 2026, which makes May 2026 the first clean post-migration month. The infra failure count covers only failures caused by the deployment system and excludes drift errors, since the two systems define drift differently. LinkedIn states that the improvement isn't solely due to the new engine. The orchestrator's error classification and reliability also got better during this time. The median duration for successful deployments is similar for both systems. However, the mean and tail have improved. The team attributes this to a namespace-scoped informer cache.

The engine is internal, and no open-source release is mentioned. Argo CD remains in use at LinkedIn for cluster add-ons and system services. The team had also found that maintaining 200+ Argo CD instances made each upgrade a multi-week project.

Teams running Argo CD at scale can check two things without a rewrite. Count the field managers on long-lived objects, since managedFields truncation can leave orphaned containers that produce no error. Then check whether sync latency tracks total pod count on shared clusters, which points to watch contention. LinkedIn concludes that the build-or-extend decision relies on the operational model. They say that per-deployment isolation, not controller tuning, allows the system to scale with compute.

LinkedIn is not the only large operator to build deployment logic around Kubernetes rather than adopt a general-purpose GitOps controller. Uber’s Up platform assigns each deployment to a dedicated controller. This is the Uber Deployment Controller. It translates the intent into Kubernetes primitives and sends status updates. This helps the workflow move forward. Uber keeps a long-running controller, while LinkedIn runs one ephemeral pod per deployment with no shared controller state.

Airbnb went further back and built its own tooling years earlier. In a talk at QCon London 2019 on InfoQ, infrastructure engineer Melanie Cebula introduced kube-gen. This internal framework creates Kubernetes configuration from one versioned project file. It also includes a deploy tool that applies or replaces objects and restarts pods, so changes take effect right away. Airbnb's deploy tool also returns an atomic success or failure, and a container that restarts for 30 seconds at the start of a rollout counts as a failed deploy. Airbnb was then at roughly 125,000 production deploys a year.

entries.title: GitHub Makes Agentic Workflows Generally Available with Isolation and Budget Controls
entries.summary: GitHub Agentic Workflows is generally available, running coding agents in GitHub Actions with read-only defaults and separately scoped write jobs. Those protections do not cover direct write permissions or custom jobs, so they depend on how each workflow is configured. By Mark Silvester
entries.content:
GitHub has made GitHub Agentic Workflows generally available. The open-source project runs coding agents inside GitHub Actions for repository tasks such as issue triage and continuous integration (CI) failure analysis. Agents start with read-only permissions, and any changes they propose are applied by separate jobs that hold their own write tokens.

That separation has limits. The project's FAQ says the protections do not automatically extend to direct write permissions or to custom jobs a workflow author adds, so the safety of a workflow depends on how it is configured. Authors can also add a GitHub Environment protection rule to require a reviewer before a write job runs.

Developers describe the work in natural-language Markdown, with YAML frontmatter for configuration. The project compiles that definition into a standard Actions workflow, which reuses existing runner groups and policy constraints, and teams can use Copilot or bring another coding agent. According to the general availability announcement, agents run in a sandboxed container behind the Agent Workflow Firewall, and a threat-detection job scans proposed changes before they are applied. The project entered public preview in June 2026.

Since the preview, GitHub has added support for Actions Runner Controller (ARC), its Kubernetes operator for self-hosted runners, with Docker-in-Docker (DinD). DinD runs a Docker daemon inside the runner pod so the agent can start its sandbox containers. The project's guide notes that ARC runs the DinD sidecar as a privileged container by default, a privileged component sitting alongside an agent designed around least privilege.

Spending is capped by default. GitHub's documentation prices AI Credits (AIC) at $0.01 each and sets a cap of 1,000 AIC ($10) per run. The project's enterprise controls reference adds defaults of 5,000 AIC a day, 400 AIC per threat-detection run and a 20-minute timeout on the agent step, all of which organisations can override. The 

gh aw forecast
command, no longer experimental, estimates monthly AI credit spending, including threat detection.

In the announcement, Ben Alton, senior manager in Accenture's Strategy, Architecture & Innovation team, said: "One of our leads saved an estimated 29 hours a week on his development work alone." The announcement does not explain how that figure was measured.

Engineers testing the project have taken a more cautious line. In a walkthrough of an issue-triage workflow, Sascha Mirow-Stanitzok, team lead for middleware at freenet, judged the default budget far too generous for triage and capped his runs at 100 AIC, 15 turns and 10 minutes. He also wrote that telling the agent to ignore instructions in issue text does not protect a workflow by itself, and said he would not use the same pattern for workflows that change code or open pull requests.

GitLab takes a different route with its Duo Agent Platform flows, which run on runners under a composite identity that pairs a service account performing the actions with the human user who started the request. Its triggers, such as a mention or an assignment, must come from a human user, so one flow cannot start another. That rule stops agents from chaining work across flows without a person starting it.

GitHub's FAQ says conventional Actions remain the right choice for reproducible builds and tests, with agent workflows suited to tasks that need interpretation or generation. The project is available on GitHub Free, Team and Enterprise on github.com, and the default Copilot CLI engine requires a Copilot licence.

entries.title: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents
entries.summary: JioHotstar evaluated 6 approaches to code retrieval for AI coding agents using SWE, CodeScale Bench, and an internal question-answering harness. Structural search performed well on concrete tasks, while semantic retrieval helped with ambiguous requirements. The findings highlight trade-offs in accuracy, token use, and tool design, underscoring the need to match retrieval tools to task types. By Le
entries.content:
JioHotstar evaluated six approaches to helping AI coding agents navigate large codebases, finding that structural code search performed well on clearly defined engineering tasks, while semantic retrieval helped more with ambiguous requirements. The evaluation also found that adding retrieval layers did not consistently improve task completion or reduce token consumption.

Abhishek Bansal, Senior Staff Engineer at JioHotStar, compared filesystem tools, Sourcebot, Graphify, CocoIndex Code, Repowise, and an in-house retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. The team evaluated the approaches using subsets of SWE-bench and CodeScaleBench, alongside a custom question-answering harness for JioHotstar's codebase. The experiments used Claude Sonnet as the solving model and measured task accuracy, token consumption, agent turns, and tool usability.

JioHotstar’s benchmark setup for evaluating code retrieval approaches for AI coding agents. (Source: JioHotstar Blog Post)

The filesystem baseline, which relied on locally checked out repositories and standard search and file operations, remained competitive on concrete tasks. Sourcebot, which provides indexed text search, symbol definitions, references, and file reads, performed better than the baseline on harder SWE-bench Verified tasks while also costing less. On simpler SWE-bench Lite tasks, retrieval generally added overhead without consistently improving results.

CodeScaleBench showed a different pattern. Semantic retrieval helped more when agents had to interpret ambiguous problem descriptions and map them to implementation details that were not obvious from exact text or symbol searches. The findings suggest that retrieval approaches should be selected according to task characteristics rather than treated as interchangeable solutions.

The report also highlighted the importance of tool design. Agents frequently preferred familiar developer operations such as searching text, reading files, and locating symbols over higher-level abstractions that required additional verification.

Tool call breakdown by category across coding agent knowledge base approaches. (Source: JioHotstar Blog Post)

Siddharth Vaithinathan raised a broader architectural question in a LinkedIn post discussing the study:

Whether coding agents should understand not only the code but also the company that produced it. He argued that repository indexing alone cannot capture why architectural decisions were made, which constraints shaped them, or what earlier incidents taught the engineering team.

Vaithinathan suggested extending agent knowledge beyond code and documentation to include architecture, constraints, decisions, rationale, incidents, and outcomes. Such context could help agents evaluate existing design choices before proposing changes, particularly in systems where historical operational experience influences architectural decisions.

Tarun Bhargava raises a relevant question for benchmark interpretation, particularly when evaluations use limited subsets and probabilistic models.

Cost/accuracy numbers with multiple runs of the same setup.

JioHotstar's evaluation did not identify a single retrieval approach that performed best across all tasks. Instead, JioHotstar recommends retaining filesystem tools as a baseline, using structural search for concrete, code-focused problems and semantic indexing for ambiguous or cross-cutting requirements. JioHotStar engineering team also emphasizes measuring tool-use traces alongside task accuracy to determine whether retrieval reduces unnecessary exploration. The findings highlight the importance of matching retrieval capabilities to the programming task and how the agent navigates the codebase.

entries.title: How LinkedIn, Netflix & DoorDash Run Agents, Evals & Inference in Production: QCon AI New York 2026
entries.summary: QCon AI New York has published its full program for December 15–16, 2026. Engineers from LinkedIn, Netflix, DoorDash, Figma, Pinterest, Honeycomb, Harvey, Google DeepMind and OpenAI describe AI systems they run in production. Talks cover agent permissions and guardrails, eval loops, inference cost, AI code review, and team adoption. By Artenisa Chatziou
entries.content:
QCon AI New York 2026 has published its full schedule for December 15–16. Engineers from LinkedIn, Netflix, DoorDash, Figma, and other organizations will examine the architecture and operational decisions behind production AI systems, including agent authorization, evaluation pipelines, model serving, and AI-assisted software delivery. With the conference a few weeks away, there is still time to join other practitioners before the full ticket price takes effect on December 9.

The program addresses questions facing teams moving beyond initial AI deployments: where to enforce agent permissions, how to connect offline evaluations to production behavior, and how to support growing inference workloads. It also examines how coding agents affect code review, engineering practices, and organizational adoption.

The following presentations explore these challenges through systems the speakers build and operate.

Keynotes

Nancy Wang, CTO at 1Password, who founded and scaled AWS Data Protection and previously worked at Rubrik and Google, opens day one with When Software Becomes a User: Identity and Authorization for Agents in Production. She argues that identity systems assume a human behind every credential, with a stable role, a bounded session, and someone accountable afterward. Agents have none of these.

Tara Sainath, Distinguished Research Scientist at Google DeepMind, lead of the Gemini Audio area and modeling lead for Project Astra, opens day two with Audio Processing with Large Language Models. She covers how LLMs have changed audio processing, and the research and product impact of audio LLMs at Google.

Agents in production

Pratik Agarwal, Distributed Systems Engineer on Figma's sandbox and caching platforms, explains how Figma provisions and secures production agents. Figma found that the trust boundary for agents extends beyond the sandbox. Warm pools cut provisioning latency by 90%, and availability rose from 99% to 99.95%.

Ronak Nathani, Principal Staff Software Engineer in Compute Infrastructure at LinkedIn and host of the Software Misadventures podcast, presents LinkedIn's Kubernetes ops agent, which works across 500,000+ nodes and 5M+ pods. Its guardrails sit on the server, including rate limits, delete protection, and peer approval for production changes.

Evals that decide whether a change ships

Fabio Flores, Software Engineer at DoorDash who leads foundation development for its agentic ordering system, explains the eval loop behind it. Every change is checked before launch by an LLM judge calibrated against human reviewers. The same rubrics score simulated and real sessions, so offline gains carry into production.

Emrick Donadei, Software Engineer on the Google DeepMind infrastructure team who works on evaluation and safety for agentic harnesses, covers agent evals the whole organization can write and keep running. The talk starts from a common problem: an eval that passes once, then fails on the next run.

Inference cost and model serving

Fan Yang, Staff Software Engineer building Netflix's AI serving platform, and Rajat Shah, Staff Software Engineer who leads the technical architecture for ML model serving, explain how Netflix serves ML and GenAI from one platform. It handles about 1 million inference requests per second across 300+ models, after five years of consolidation. They cover what multi-tenancy costs to operate.

Salina Wu, Software Engineer building Pinterest's generative AI serving platform, and Cristian Lopez, Software Engineer on GenAI Serving at Pinterest, present Pinterest's vision-language model serving stack on NVIDIA Dynamo. It is built for multimodal workloads with heavy prefill computation and large KV cache pressure.

AI-assisted software engineering

Min Chen, Principal Staff Engineer at LinkedIn with more than 25 years of software development experience, presents LinkedIn's AI code review system. It reviews tens of thousands of pull requests a week across about 10,000 repositories. More than 60% of sampled suggestions are accepted, and a validation pipeline filters findings before developers see them.

Joey Wang, engineering lead at Harvey who created Spectre, Harvey's internal collaborative cloud agent platform, explains how Harvey shipped its agents internally first on Spectre. Spectre passed 7,000 merged pull requests across every repository before the agents reached lawyers.

Engineering leadership and adoption

Liz Fong-Jones, Technical Fellow at Honeycomb and site reliability engineer with more than two decades of experience, and Rebecca Murphey, Principal for AI Ops at Honeycomb and author of Build: Elements of an Effective Software Organization, reflect on Honeycomb's 2x initiative. Peak weekday PR merges to Honeycomb's main monorepo rose from about 30 to about 74 between early 2025 and April 2026, and have held steady since.

Brian Yang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI who builds AI-native advertising and monetization systems, covers making AI adoption work across an engineering team. He looks at what happens after every engineer has coding agents, when one person finds a way of working that teammates struggle to reproduce.

Also on the program

Other sessions come from engineers at Anthropic, Microsoft, BlackRock, Databricks, Datadog, Tessl, LangChain, Baseten, and Google Cloud’s DORA team. Topics include agentic standards, sandbox density, SRE agents, AgentOps for financial services, inference with vLLM, voice agents, software factories, and enterprise AI adoption.
