entries.title: Presentation: Uncorking Queueing Bottlenecks with OpenTelemetry
entries.summary: Oli Lane and Julian Wreford share how Gearset replaced guesswork in distributed asynchronous queues with OpenTelemetry tracing. They explain why traditional metrics fall short, how to implement user-centric SLOs based on latency distributions, and share practical debugging tips to help senior developers, software architects, and engineering leaders improve system reliability and team culture. By J
entries.content:
Transcript

Oli Lane: A few years back, I have this really vivid memory of a customer complaint coming in. It was late on a Friday, of course, they always are. I was just letting my mind wander towards the pub, and this message comes through. It's a big customer, it's a customer we need to keep happy. They said, my backup job ran like an hour late, what's going on? They were pretty annoyed, rightly so, they need to trust that our backup product works, and it's solid and it's dependable. Of course, we dug in. We had our dashboards. We had our metrics. We had our logs. We had our alerts. We did some rooting around, we came up with some plausible theories. We put in a few fixes, a few improvements to make sure that any of the things that we suspected it was wouldn't happen again. I got to the pub a bit late, end of story.

There was this thing that didn't sit right with me and it was that we never really figured out the most important question, which was, why did that job run late and why was it late that time? It was like a murder mystery with the last chapter ripped out. It really annoyed me. This talk is the story of getting from there, where we're squinting at graphs and making a good guess, but mostly shrugging to being able to point and explain the exact bottleneck in a distributed asynchronous system.

Background

I'm Oli. I'm an engineering team lead at Gearset. I've worn many hats, but recently I've been focused on levelling up our observability and our incident response and our team culture as well so that we can build reliable, dependable software, especially as we scale.

Julian Wreford: I'm Julian. I've been part of Oli's team for the last three years as we've built out those observability tools and recently stepped into the team lead role for the team that Oli's been leading.

Oli Lane: From this talk, we're hoping you'll take away a practical knowledge of how to better understand the performance characteristics of your queues in particular, and we'll go through the foundations of OpenTelemetry and build on that to explain practical strategies that we've used to turn our queues from that point of confusion within our teams to something that we really feel confident running in production. We'll discuss different strategies to measure queue health, and then we'll finish off with some tips and tricks that we really wish someone had told us when we were getting started. You should go away better equipped to understand why metrics and logs aren't enough to truly understand your async workflows and how OpenTelemetry might help, how to know when your queue is healthy or unhealthy. How to empower your teams to measure and debug how customers are experiencing your system, and how to take that next step and get your teams adopting this stuff.

Why Queues?

Let's take a step back for a minute. Why do we need queues in the first place? Your system probably doesn't start with a queue right from day one. If you've got queues, you probably added them after hitting either a pain point or to resolve some architectural problem. For us, we started with all our code in a single monolith, looked a bit like that. We had multiple replicas of that monolith but only one image that actually shipped. At some point, we needed to organize that better and we decided to split off a few things to handle different responsibilities. Specifically, we wanted our scheduling code, so that was the code that was responsible for kicking off user jobs at specific times. We wanted that to run separately from our core application code. We did that in the simplest way possible. We spun up a new service, it had its own database.

To begin with, it would just poke a HTTP endpoint on the core app and it would kick off a job. Simple enough. That was a good start, but it had some immediate problems and some of these might feel familiar. We had no ability to smooth the load. We had a whole load of customer workloads configured on the scheduler, and one of those workloads was backups, and we let people pick when they wanted to run their backup. I don't know if you've ever given people a date, time picker for their backups but almost everyone picks midnight. Unfortunately, that meant that at midnight, our scheduler would suddenly DoS our application code with hundreds of requests to start some really heavy jobs in parallel. We could work around this in some ways. We could scale the application code or we could put bodges in the producer code and try and throttle it.

We could take the choice away from the users. Ultimately, these spikes were causing problems and we had no real way of dealing with them properly. Then, also, the workloads weren't truly decoupled. When you synchronously call via HTTP from one service to another and you expect a response, you still, in some ways, have a hard dependency between those services. One has to be up for the other one to work properly. We wanted to be able to take the app down without worrying whether the scheduler was up and what it was doing. Queues could solve both of those problems. Queues smoothed the load without the producer needing to know anything about the consumer. The scheduler could just dump a few hundred jobs on the queue and those consumers could pick them up at their leisure with sensible concurrency limits. Queues meant that if the consumers went down, we could build up a backlog and we could just let the app catch up when it got back online. These are not the only reasons you might introduce queues, but they were the main drivers for us. Of course, once we had one queue, everything looked like a nail and we had plenty of other sensible places to add our queues.

The next problem, as soon as you've got queues, is how to figure out if your queues are happy. We all know that software will always go wrong if it has a chance to. Whatever queuing technology you're using, whether it's SQS, Kafka, Rabbit, something else, you'll get some metrics emitted out of the box. These are some of the most common ones you'll have to work with. Queue size, the number of items currently on the queue. The enqueue rate, so how many items are being queued per time period. Dequeue rate, how many are being taken off per time period. Then the in-flight count, which is just how many are currently being processed. The basic idea here is if your enqueue rate is consistently higher than your dequeue rate, you're putting more into the bucket than you're taking out, and the queue size is going to grow. That could happen for loads of reasons.

Maybe half of your consumers blow up. Maybe you had got a big spike of traffic. Maybe the average time to process a message has gone up. When queue size is growing, messages are probably getting delayed, workloads are probably waiting, things are probably bad. That seemed like a good place to start, and we started monitoring those metrics. That went ok for a while. We ended up with tens of queues across multiple regions, and our monitoring was getting a little bit unwieldy, so we built these Grafana dashboards that grew and grew and grew, and some of them were more usable than others might be familiar.

Metrics Limits

One thing we noticed was that all of these queues weren't created equal. There were some queues where we were fine with the delay. They were the jobs which, ultimately, they ran in the background, and a few minutes of delay, not a problem, as long as they get done. There are some queues where delays would be noticeable for users. To keep track of what was healthy and what wasn't, we added alerting to the metrics that we had, but we had to tune each one of those based on the number of consumers that we expected and how large we were happy with that queue growing. Along the way, we did add one small improvement to the default metrics that we got out of the box. We created our own metric that measured how long the message had been on the queue, so when a message was received, we'd look at when that message was sent, and we'd calculate how long has that message been on the queue, and we'd track that, too.

You might get that out of the box, but we didn't. That meant we had the high-level view at any given time of what state the queue was in. We knew if it was backing up, and we knew if it was delaying workloads. That was good, but when something did start going wrong, our alerts are firing, metrics would tell us roughly where to look, but they wouldn't tell us much more. For more detail, we had to look in our logs, and that ended up meaning a lot of manual work. We'd sometimes burn hours chasing a phantom spike, and we'd never be particularly confident about any conclusion that we really came to. In a simple system, that manual work is probably tractable, but in a distributed system with lots of interconnected parts as it grows, it can quickly become an impossible task as your product scales.

OpenTelemetry Tracing Fundamentals

Julian Wreford: This was the point where we realized we needed to probably do something different. Our metrics were giving us the big picture, but they weren't giving us a whole lot more than that. If we had to follow up on questions, we couldn't ask them in hindsight without adding in more metrics and waiting for the issue to happen again. Metrics would give us the forest, but not the trees. Equally, our logs gave us plenty of detail at the level of each component of our system, but they were hard to connect to the wider picture. They were also very hard to follow through multiple components for complex requests, so they gave us the trees without the forest. We needed something that would do a bit different and go somewhere in the middle. Of course, we aren't the only people having these problems. A whole community sprung up around the idea of observability and how to inspect, debug, and operate complex systems.

The technology most people land on is OpenTelemetry. It's an open-source protocol, which allows you to do a lot of things, but for the purpose of this talk, we're going to focus on its support for distributed tracing. Distributed tracing, you can think of it a little like structured logs. We all know what a log is, and structured logs do what they say on the tin. They let you pass not just a string, but a structured set of keys and values, which allows you to query and filter the events a bit more easily. Traces are very similar, in that they are also made of a bunch of structured events with arbitrary keys and values. What traces have over structured logs is the ability to assign a hierarchy to those events, even when the events are produced by different parts of your system. The hierarchy allows you to group all of the events that stem from a single operation or customer request.

Logging this would probably be called like a correlation ID, but it also allows you to get a sense of the cause and effect relationship between events. What was the full sequence of events that led to an error or a delay? Which systems did the request pass through before this one? Of course, it's called distributed tracing, because this hierarchy can be preserved and reconstructed, even when different components are omitting different parts of the trace.

This is what a very simple trace might look like. You have a route span, which represents some interaction with an entry point to your system. This might be a customer hitting your API, and a number of child spans, which represent the activities that the system has to do to respond to the request. These spans might represent things like database requests, calls to other systems, or specific functions developers are interested in, and have added their own telemetry for. There are two interesting things here. One is the arrows representing the hierarchy of cause and effect, and the other is the horizontal axis, which represents the time, so we can see how long each duration lasted. Each of these spans has a name, which we've written in each box, but they can also have any other arbitrary attributes attached to them for analysis or querying purposes, and we want to make those as wide as possible.

The spans are connected by three special attributes defined by the OTel standard. There's the trace ID, which means that we can associate the span with the trace it belongs to, the span ID, which uniquely identifies the span itself, and the parent ID, which identifies which span preceded this one. All spans have a parent, apart from the route, which is defined by having no parent at all. This simple association of spans allows you to build up these tree-like structures that can be paired with a query engine, which allows us to query not just across spans, but also their relationships. As I'm sure many of you all know, OpenTelemetry support has grown rapidly across our ecosystems, and for us in the world of C#, there was good support straight out of the box. It didn't take us long to start seeing the value of how lots of operations connected to form a single customer request.

We even saw the traces automatically carrying on over HTTP boundaries. The trace above shows a parent span in our data service in the U.S. data residency region, which has a child on a completely different service, on a completely different region, because it's made a HTTP call out to that service. This is a screenshot from our query engine specifically. We use Honeycomb to analyze our trace data. You'll be seeing a bunch of screenshots from it in the rest of the talk. We're big fans of Honeycomb as a product, but there are other providers that offer similar things and they'll ingest OTel in similar ways.

That was HTTP calls, but when it came to following traces through queues, things weren't quite so plug and play. In the early days, it wouldn't be uncommon for us to have to jump through three or four traces to find the full context of what was happening, and that made it really hard for us to understand the full flow of information around our systems. We were in a better position than we were with logs, because we could track a request per system, but we couldn't easily get one big picture of the request as a whole. Helpfully, this is the exact problem that OpenTelemetry was designed to deal with. It defines a standard to allow context propagation to happen, so that traces can be rebuilt from spans that are created across a number of different systems, while being language-independent. This is built into the SDKs and library in most cases, which is why it works across HTTP boundaries in the last slide.

In the case of our queues, we need a little bit of work ourselves, because the libraries we had didn't speak OTel natively. For that to work, we had to propagate two things between systems. One is the traceparent, which is a simple string which combines four different things in a hyphenated format. The version of the OpenTelemetry being used, this is just 01 for us at the moment. The trace ID, which is what the span should be a part of, so that the trace can be continued on the customer side. The parent span ID, which is the span that's active on the sending system before the message was sent. This then becomes the parent span ID of the first span on the consumer side, so that you can connect the things up. Finally, the trace flags. These are the communication of defined flags across systems. Right now, the only trace flag defined in the spec is whether a span should be recorded, and that means that you're going to find whether a whole trace should or shouldn't be recorded, and you don't get partial results.

You can sample at the top level, and that will come through all of your systems. That's the traceparent. The second part is the tracestate. This is a simple key-value list, which comes in handy in a few contexts we'll talk about later. In our case, to propagate these two things, we wrote a small middleware layer for our queuing clients on both producer and receiver sides. Before sending a message, we generate the trace context, attach it as metadata to the message, and then when we're picking that message up again, we'd pass that metadata out, plug that back into the native C# library. Jobs are good.

While we're at it in the middleware, we also added a bunch of useful attributes, which would help our system become more useful for querying. The OTel specs, just a few, like messaging.destination.name, the operation name, and the system. We also added a few of our own as well. Created, sent, and received timestamps mean that we can do calculations on the Honeycomb side to calculate the amount of time it took between the message being sent and received, meaning that we can replicate that message delay metric we talked about earlier. The subgroup ID, which we use for SQS FIFO queues, that mean we can see concurrency at the subgroup ID level and understand blockages caused by the FIFO part of the queue rather than the overall queue concurrency. Immediately after that, immediately after we put this in the middleware, we're able to see the full lifetime of requests bouncing around our system.

The image here shows three hops that we make. Right at the top, the webhook proxy enqueue service receives a POST request from the outside world. It does some simple validation of our database and pops the message onto our first queue, the webhook proxy pipeline. Then the dequeue service picks up that message and proxies it onto the pipeline service via a POST request. The pipeline service does some initial processing, and after that, puts the message onto another queue, which is then processed by a different pipeline service pod. Being able to visualize this whole operation meant we could understand the complex sequence of events that were going on in our system for any given request. Another nice outcome was that we could have a high-level visualization of the interconnectivity of all of our services. This is a simplified diagram that's based off our actual trace data. It shows the number of spans between two services, but also allows us to visualize the average latency between any given services.

One of our biggest surprises with the introduction of tracing was just how much waste it exposed in our systems. When we were able to graph every single connection between services and every single database query, we realized there were a bunch of unknowns we'd never even quantified before. For example, we looked at one of our busiest queues, one which had caused us pain for multiple years at this point, which regularly needed its capacity in peak hours. With the tooling we now had, we realized that the source for almost all of our longest-running messages was for a legacy piece of code, which we didn't really need any more. We were able to ship a small fix that removed a dependency we didn't realize we had, and suddenly that queue had ample capacity at all hours of day, and we stopped needing to worry about scaling on that side of the world.

It was shocking how much insight we gained into systems which we thought we were already the experts in. We had no idea how many unknown unknowns had been lurking in our production systems' behavior. Once the fog had lifted, we were really able to dig in and fully bottom out the edge cases and make much more informed decisions about how we wanted our systems to work.

Is My Queue Healthy?

Oli Lane: The telemetry was invaluable to help us diagnose issues when they were reported to us, but we firmly believe our aim should be to detect problems before customers notice them. We don't want to be reactive to customer issues. We want to be proactive. How do you know when a customer's experiencing pain? How do you know when it's serious enough to investigate? We'd been doing ok with our alerts based on those initial CloudWatch metrics, but now we've got all this extra trace data, how can we level up our alerting with all of that data, especially for our queues? We want to know whether a queue is healthy or not, but what healthy actually means will differ from use case to use case, like I mentioned earlier. There are loads of things you can measure. Here's a selection of the most important ones. Error rates, how many messages are successfully or unsuccessfully handled?

Processing time, how long does it take to process one message? Throughput, how many messages are being processed in a given time period? Latency, how long are we waiting on each message? Queue size. We've talked about queue size. The thing to notice here is that they're all interrelated. For example, if processing time for each message goes up, but you didn't add any extra consumers, you'd expect throughput to go down, and then you'd expect the queue size to go up. Once the queue size goes up, you'd expect that to increase the latency. It's a fairly complex but intuitive link, but there's counterintuitive links here as well. For example, if you ship a bug that causes loads of errors, you might actually see all of the other metrics improve because maybe it takes less time to process a failure than to properly run a job. There's dragons here.

What do we alert on? Error rates seem pretty obvious. We basically always want to know if suddenly all of our messages are failing to process. The rest of these are a little harder to pin down. Most queue providers make it very easy to monitor the queue size. A lot of people start with that, us included. If the queue size gets too big, something's wrong. It works, but it's got some drawbacks. Firstly, it's really hard to tune. What counts as too many messages on the queue is very context dependent. You could have a thousand items on your queue that all get processed really quickly, or you could have five that get processed really slowly. Each time your system characteristics change, for example, you acquire new customers and you scale your infrastructure and move things around a little bit, you might have to retune all of your alerts.

Secondly, it's not particularly well tied to customer experience. The customer doesn't care that there's a thousand other items in the queue. What they probably care about is when their item's going to be processed. Thinking about that probably gets us to a better thing to measure. Funnily enough, a great analogy here is Google Maps. When there's traffic on your route, Google Maps is essentially alerting you to an unhealthy queue, but notice what metric it uses to tell you how bad it is. It uses the latency. How many extra minutes is this going to add to your journey? Google probably has the data to tell you how many cars per minute are passing through that traffic jam, how many cars are waiting on that particular stretch of road, how many lanes are open. Some of those are probably interesting, but the most interesting thing is how long you're going to wait.

We switched over from alerting mainly on queue size to alerting mainly on latency, and we found that much easier to make our alerts useful but also actionable. That's for two main reasons. An alert means that a customer genuinely had a bad time. They waited longer than what we have defined as the acceptable maximum wait. Secondly, we don't have to retune that alert when the system changes, because the acceptable delay is still the same. The customer expectation is still the same. Actually, this reasoning applies to pretty much everything you're going to alert on, not just queues. Measuring something as close as possible to a real aspect of the user experience is always going to give you a more actionable alert. We've decided we're going to alert mostly on latency. The next problem we run into is that almost all of these measures are distributions. Treating them as one number by taking an average loses information.

Let's say our metric is saying the latency is 3 seconds. That could be either of these situations. It could mean that every message is delayed exactly 3 seconds, or that most are faster but some subset are much slower, or a hundred in between. Aggregating to a single number is lossy. Why does that matter? It's important to us for a few reasons. We run our services across multiple regions, but ideally, we want a single alert per queue type because the customer experience shouldn't change between regions. It shouldn't matter which region you're hitting if it has thousands of customers or hundreds of customers. Those different parts of that distribution do matter to us. We run a multi-tenant architecture, and as Julian mentioned, we use subgroups to create fairness across our queues. That means that sometimes we do expect some customers to have an extra delay if they introduce a big spike of workload.

The rest of our customers should be protected from that spike, but also, we need to keep a track of how much that fairness algorithm is affecting the customer that's put on a big spike of workload. We do care about every customer. It's not enough for us if 80% of our customers are having a great time at the expense of 20% who aren't. At the same time, we do have to be careful. Our systems are never going to be perfect and we don't really want to alert if one single customer goes one millisecond over our latency limit. We want to take into account the full distribution, but perhaps we want some soft edges to avoid noisy alerts.

How do we square the circle? We landed on service level objectives, SLOs. The good news is that we've got all of that underlying distribution data, not just an aggregate or a coarse histogram. We can build more nuance into our strategy. We could do a whole talk on SLOs, but we'll just cover the basics here and how they help us to solve that distribution problem. Essentially, the idea here is that we define a bar between this is a good event and this is a bad event. Then, we can define targets and budgets for how many good and bad events we want to see. Let's imagine we have this whole bucket of events coming through, they're all different shapes and sizes. The first thing we're going to do is to define an SLI or a service level indicator. The job of the SLI is to bucket our events into the acceptable or not acceptable buckets.

For our queuing example, we might say that a message on a particular queue is a good event if it's processed within 2 seconds and a bad event if it's taken more than 2 seconds. Easy enough. We can define that as a simple formula, and that gets calculated as our events roll in. The nice thing about working with all the data here is that we can be as simple or as complex as we want with that definition. It can be as simple as slow is bad, or it can loop in extra conditions around different customer types, different workloads. For example, if you want to define a single SLI that has different latency expectations for different types of HTTP endpoints, you can do that. If you want a different expectation on a different day of the week, you can do that for a different region, whatever. It's really flexible. Now that we've bucketed our events, we can move on to defining the actual alert.

Generally, we think of these in terms of an error budget. We've got our SLI, and we want to set our SLO, our objective. What proportion of those spans do we expect to be good? Therefore, how many can be bad before we run out of an error budget? We might decide to be really strict and expect to have 99.99% good, or we might say 95% is fine. Either way, we're able to work with our product teams to help define what good means for this customer use case, and then we can work backwards and codify that within our alerts. Once you have that budget, we can define an alert that fires when the budget's exhausted, but also, we can define an alert when there's been a shift in the burn rate that would mean the SLO would be breached in some number of hours. That allows us to be sensitive and rapidly alerted to changes in behavior, while also making sure the alert doesn't fire too much for false positives and individual spikes.

The real superpower here is how it's integrated with the rest of the trace data. Once an alert fires, we immediately have visualizations of the distribution of events, and we can go straight from that macro view into specific examples of problem traces that failed the test, and we can see if we can work out what happened. Because the system already knows what we've defined as good and bad in terms of these events, we can quickly group by that definition and see what's different about the events that are slow, or returning errors, or whatever the problem is. That's the value of having these really wide, rich events which can be aggregated in an exploratory way on the fly.

Putting it All Together

Julian Wreford: This is a little abstract so far, so let's dig into a little bit of how this all fits together in practice. Imagine it's a Friday afternoon and your head started drifting towards the pub again, when suddenly an alert comes into Slack. We're seeing queue delays and customer experience is probably affected. Immediately on each message, we're able to see what the affected queue is, what the expected queue delay is. In this case it's one of our real-time queues which we expect to be almost instant, and how long we've got until the SLO budget will expire. This puts us in a good place and means we can jump into investigation mode. Immediately we can jump in and from the SLO we can see the amount of delay each message is experiencing. We clearly had a short spike at 5:15, and one a bit after 5:30. Note that the delay is in minutes on the axis and we're aiming for sub-1 second latency, so these delays are definitely going to be starting to feel painful for our customers.

We can also see the number of concurrent spans for that queue, that is the number of messages being processed at that point by our systems. We've got a couple of flat caps at the same time as the queue delays. This is when we've hit the system capacity and so there's a backlog of messages building up on the queue because we can't handle them as fast as they're coming in. Before we start diagnosing the problem, it's worth mentioning our guiding logic which is that stable systems stay stable until something changes. When we see our system becoming unstable, we need to figure out what changed. For us that tends to be three buckets. We could have broken something, could be that we've shipped a bug which has created more messages than normal, or we've changed the dequeue side to be too slow to process the messages, or even we might have slowed down a downstream dependency somewhere else which might be a completely different bit of code entirely.

Our users could be doing something different. Either an individual user might have suddenly produced a large spike, or we may have naturally acquired enough customers that the group as a whole pushed us to our infrastructure limits at our peak time. Or a third party could be causing problems. The nature of our product means that we're quite reliant on Salesforce and GitHub and a number of different version control providers. If one of those is running slowly, we can also have a downstream effect on our ability to process workloads and some will go slower. If we start with the first one, have we broken something? In queuing systems, the two causes of delay tend to be either we've produced something significant in our workload or the consumer isn't able to keep up.
